objective: Assess the security posture of the Docker environment hosting a containerized industrial control system (ICS) lab. Identify container misconfigurations, risky network exposure, missing resource limits, and known image vulnerabilities. Prioritise risks by their impact on an OT environment and give concrete, evidence-based remediation for defenders.

summary.executive_summary: The Docker environment hosting the ICS lab has critical vulnerabilities in multiple images used by exposed services, including the Docker socket mounted in a container. High-severity issues in images like 'ics_range-hmi:latest' and 'ics_range-wazuh-manager:latest' pose immediate risks to availability and integrity. The 'shuffle-backend' container's access to the Docker socket is a critical misconfiguration requiring urgent remediation.

findings.title: Docker socket is mounted into the container

evidence.note: even a read-only mount of the socket allows full API use

findings.explanation: The Docker API socket grants full control of the Docker daemon: anyone who controls this container can start a privileged container that mounts the host filesystem, i.e. root on the host and control of every ICS component. Mounting it ':ro' does NOT help - it only makes the socket file read-only, not the API.
findings.remediation: Remove the socket mount. If the service needs Docker metadata (e.g. a version/status page), give it a filtered read-only proxy such as tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy with POST=0 and only the needed API sections.

findings.title: Container runs as root (container is currently exited)
findings.explanation: The main process runs as UID 0. Combined with any added capability, writable mount or kernel bug, root inside the container makes escape and host compromise significantly easier.
findings.remediation: Add a non-root `USER` to the Dockerfile (or `user: "1000:1000"` in compose) and fix file ownership so the service runs unprivileged. Consider user-namespace remapping (`userns-remap`) on the daemon.

findings.title: Container adds dangerous capabilities: NET_ADMIN, NET_RAW (container is currently exited)

evidence.note: can reconfigure interfaces, routes and firewall rules
can craft raw packets (spoofing, ARP poisoning on the ICS segment)

findings.explanation: Added capabilities widen what a compromised process can do to the host kernel and network. In an OT lab, NET_ADMIN/NET_RAW on hosts attached to the process network allow traffic manipulation between PLCs and HMIs.
findings.remediation: Remove capabilities that are not strictly required. Start from `cap_drop: [ALL]` and add back only what the service needs; if NET_ADMIN is only used at start-up (e.g. to add routes), configure networking outside the container instead.

findings.title: Credential-like environment variables: POSTGRES_PASSWORD (container is currently exited)
findings.explanation: Secrets passed as environment variables are visible to anyone who can inspect the container (docker inspect, /proc/<pid>/environ) and often leak into logs and crash dumps. Values were redacted and not analysed; the name alone indicates a likely credential.
findings.remediation: Use Docker secrets / mounted secret files with restricted permissions, and rotate any credential that was exposed via the environment.

findings.title: Container bridges multiple networks
findings.explanation: A container attached to several networks is a potential bridge between segmentation zones (e.g. DMZ <-> process network). If it is compromised, an attacker can pivot across zones that the network design intends to keep apart. Whether this is intended (a router/firewall) needs human review.
findings.remediation: Attach the container only to the networks it must serve. Route inter-zone traffic through a dedicated, hardened firewall container and keep management networks separate from ICS process networks.

findings.title: no-new-privileges is not set (container is currently exited)
findings.explanation: Without no-new-privileges, setuid/setgid binaries inside the container can raise a process's privileges.
findings.remediation: Add `security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]`.

findings.title: Root filesystem is writable (container is currently exited)
findings.explanation: A writable root filesystem lets an attacker persist tools or modify binaries/configuration (e.g. PLC logic or HMI screens) inside the container.
findings.remediation: Set `read_only: true` and mount `tmpfs` / named volumes only for the paths that must be writable.

findings.title: Ports published on all host interfaces (container is currently exited)
findings.explanation: These ports are reachable from every network the Docker host is attached to. This is an EXPOSURE observation, not a vulnerability by itself: risk depends on the service behind the port (see image vulnerabilities and authentication). ICS management interfaces (HMI, PLC web UI, engineering tools) should not be reachable from untrusted networks.
findings.remediation: Bind to loopback or a management interface (`127.0.0.1:8080:8080`) or remove the port mapping and reach the service via an internal network / jump host.

findings.title: Missing resource limits: memory, cpu, pids (container is currently exited)
findings.explanation: Without limits, one runaway or compromised container can exhaust host memory/CPU/PIDs and starve every other ICS component (availability is the top priority in OT environments).
findings.remediation: Set `mem_limit`, `cpus` and `pids_limit` (compose) or `deploy.resources.limits` appropriate to each service.

findings.remediation: Set `read_only: true` and mount `tmpfs` / named volumes only for the paths that must be writable.

findings.title: Ports published on all host interfaces
findings.explanation: These ports are reachable from every network the Docker host is attached to. This is an EXPOSURE observation, not a vulnerability by itself: risk depends on the service behind the port (see image vulnerabilities and authentication). ICS management interfaces (HMI, PLC web UI, engineering tools) should not be reachable from untrusted networks.
findings.remediation: Bind to loopback or a management interface (`127.0.0.1:8080:8080`) or remove the port mapping and reach the service via an internal network / jump host.

findings.title: Missing resource limits: memory, cpu, pids
findings.explanation: Without limits, one runaway or compromised container can exhaust host memory/CPU/PIDs and starve every other ICS component (availability is the top priority in OT environments).
findings.remediation: Set `mem_limit`, `cpus` and `pids_limit` (compose) or `deploy.resources.limits` appropriate to each service.

findings.title: no-new-privileges is not set
findings.explanation: Without no-new-privileges, setuid/setgid binaries inside the container can raise a process's privileges.
findings.remediation: Add `security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]`.

findings.title: Image uses a floating tag: ics_range-admin-ui:latest
findings.explanation: `latest`/untagged images change silently when rebuilt or re-pulled, so the deployed software (and its vulnerabilities) is not reproducible or auditable.
findings.remediation: Pin images to an explicit version tag and, ideally, an immutable digest (`image: repo/name:1.2.3@sha256:...`).

findings.title: No capabilities are dropped (container is currently exited)
findings.explanation: The container keeps Docker's full default capability set (incl. NET_RAW, CHOWN, SETUID...). Most services need none of these.
findings.remediation: Add `cap_drop: [ALL]` and re-add only required capabilities.

potential_concerns.explanation: The process simulator may be bridging networks without proper segmentation, increasing attack surface.

prioritized.rationale: The Docker socket mount in 'shuffle-backend' allows container escape, which could compromise the entire host and ICS processes. This is a top priority in OT environments where integrity of control systems is critical.

recommendations: Immediately remove the Docker socket mount from 'shuffle-backend' by modifying its Dockerfile or runtime configuration.
Update all vulnerable images (e.g., 'ics_range-hmi:latest', 'ics_range-wazuh-manager:latest') to versions with fixed CVEs.
Implement resource limits for Elasticsearch and other critical services to prevent DoS.
Isolate the 'ics_range-process-simulator:latest' container to a dedicated network with strict access controls.
Scan all remaining images with Trivy to identify and remediate additional vulnerabilities.
limitations: Metadata-only assessment: no runtime behaviour, network traffic or in-container files were inspected, and no active scanning was performed.
Image vulnerabilities come from Trivy's database at scan time; exploitability depends on whether the vulnerable code is reachable, which was not tested.
Secret values were redacted before analysis; credential findings are based on variable names and patterns only.
Findings reflect the Docker state at the snapshot time only; historical runs are not evidence of current state.
Only 19 of 162 findings are shown; lower-severity issues may exist but are not prioritized here.
Network topology details (e.g., bridge configurations) are not available to fully assess segmentation risks.
